ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly medium-to-long turns: brief, casual check-ins and technical troubleshooting at the start give way to extended, presentation-style monologues and detailed audience questions. Overlap is occasional but not disruptive, often appearing as quick acknowledgments, laughter-like reactions, or participants jumping in with “yeah,” “okay,” and “right.” The tone is collegial and semi-formal—professional during introductions and research discussion, but relaxed, warm, and joking in transitions. Speakers hedge frequently with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “you know,” “maybe,” “I guess,” and “it could be,” especially when interpreting results or posing open questions. Contributions commonly build on prior remarks by restating part of the previous point before extending it; challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity or uncertainty rather than disagreement. Speech is highly spontaneous, with fillers, repetitions, false starts, self-corrections, incomplete sentences, and occasional grammar slips, particularly from nonnative speakers. Questions tend to be prefaced with praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “just curious”), then unfold as multi-part exploratory questions rather than concise interrogatives.

Meeting style for this meeting (running_out_of_time): The meeting starts late or the agenda is too long. People keep an eye on the clock, cut themselves off, skip items, and the meeting ends with things unfinished. No final recap.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - We've got maybe fifteen minutes, so- can we skip the intro stuff?
  - Yeah, sure. Let's just start with what's blocking.
  - I really have to jump in about five, sorry.
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Setting up wastewater monitoring for infectious disease in a mid-sized city and deciding who sees the data.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Patel
speakers.background: Dr. Patel is an applied infectious-disease epidemiologist with 11 years of experience building surveillance systems for city and state health agencies. Her work combines time-series analysis, outbreak detection, syndromic surveillance, and evaluation of surveillance sensitivity and timeliness. She has collaborated with laboratories and utilities on wastewater-derived indicators but is careful about translating population-level signals into public-health claims. In the pilot, she is responsible for defining how wastewater trends will be compared with aggregate clinical indicators and how findings are framed for health-department decision-makers.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats wastewater monitoring as a complementary surveillance stream rather than a direct count of infections. She emphasizes that apparent lead time depends on pathogen shedding, sampling cadence, reporting delays, and changing clinical testing behavior; it should be estimated locally rather than assumed. She wants normalization choices to be explicit and sensitivity-tested against flow and population proxies, and insists that interceptor signals describe a catchment-level aggregate, not a building, block, school, or household. She supports the provisional citywide dashboard with categorized trends and methods notes, while asking what evidence would make a signal interpretable enough to alter operational awareness without overstating certainty.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Lionel Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is an STS scholar and former public-sector program evaluator with 9 years of experience studying data infrastructures, public-health expertise, and community participation in environmental monitoring. He has conducted interviews, document analysis, meeting ethnography, and comparative case studies of how agencies turn uncertain measurements into public facts. As project manager, he tracks decisions that are being embedded in the pilot design, including who receives information, who can interpret anomalies, and how the team accounts for affected communities.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He approaches the pilot as a sociotechnical system in which credibility is produced through instruments, laboratory protocols, institutional roles, communication practices, and opportunities to contest interpretation. He asks whose expertise is authorized when an interceptor trend is unusual, how uncertainty is made visible rather than merely managed internally, and whether restricted reporting can unintentionally mark smaller catchments as objects of surveillance rather than participants in governance. He supports beginning with a weekly citywide dashboard and limited operational access to interceptor results during evaluation, but views that arrangement as a provisional governance choice requiring explicit authority, review criteria, and meaningful consideration of community representation.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Elena Morales
speakers.background: Elena is a fourth-year environmental engineering PhD student working with municipal utilities on wastewater pathogen surveillance. She has two years of field experience coordinating autosamplers, chain-of-custody procedures, cold-storage logistics, and RT-qPCR workflows, along with analysis of plant flow records, rainfall effects, and industrial discharge patterns. Her dissertation evaluates how sampling frequency, composite collection, and laboratory reporting thresholds affect whether wastewater trends can be distinguished from measurement noise. She is leading the pilot's sampling-plan validation and laboratory quality-control documentation.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She starts with what the system can reliably measure under real operating conditions. For Riverton, she sees the design choice as a tradeoff between temporal resolution at the main plant and geographic resolution from the two smaller interceptors. She emphasizes that wet-weather dilution, changing flow, industrial inputs, sample hold time, extraction efficiency, and assay variability can all change a reported concentration before it becomes an epidemiologic trend. She wants each result tied to clear quality-control flags and a quantified detection limit where feasible, and is cautious about treating low or intermittent interceptor detections as meaningful without repeat observations and operational context. She accepts the citywide-dashboard and restricted-interceptor approach for the pilot, provided the data-release plan does not imply more precision than the sampling and laboratory system can support.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

meeting_opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary research meeting with sufficient topic context for the evaluated AI to recommend related literature offering a new viewpoint. Record existing perspectives so novelty can be assessed. Do not fabricate publications; recommended literature needs external verification.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary research meeting with sufficient topic context for the evaluated AI to recommend related literature offering a new viewpoint. Record existing perspectives so novelty can be assessed. Do not fabricate publications; recommended literature needs external verification.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning discussion among an epidemiologist, an environmental engineer, and an STS researcher. The epidemiologist should state the value and limits of lead time, normalization, catchment interpretation, and comparison with clinical indicators. The engineer should state the sampling, flow/dilution, laboratory, and detection-limit constraints behind the two sampling designs. The STS researcher should state concerns about expertise, uncertainty communication, public fact-making, infrastructure, and trust. The group should confirm the provisional citywide-dashboard/restricted-interceptor-data approach and identify the unresolved governance questions about interpretation authority, release criteria, and community participation. No participant should recommend specific publications or claim that a particular literature resolves the questions; the later evaluated AI must generate externally verifiable literature recommendations. Keep the discussion focused on the pilot rather than creating a hidden dispute or a final governance decision.

existing_perspectives: Epidemiologic surveillance perspective: wastewater may provide lead time over clinical reporting, but its interpretation requires normalization, defensible catchment definitions, detection limits, and careful comparison with clinical indicators affected by testing behavior.

Environmental engineering perspective: site selection, composite-sampling frequency, sewer flow, rainfall dilution, industrial discharges, preservation, laboratory method choice, and quantified detection limits determine what signals can credibly mean.

STS perspective: data credibility and legitimacy depend on who is recognized as an expert, how uncertainty becomes publicly communicable knowledge, how infrastructure shapes the evidence, and how disclosure choices affect trust and representation.
ground_truth.opportunity_for_new_viewpoint: Literature recommendations should add a perspective that is meaningfully distinct from the three recorded perspectives, rather than merely supplying more wastewater assay validation, epidemiologic lead-time studies, or general trust/governance commentary. Promising distinct lenses may include data justice and distributive consequences of spatially granular surveillance; public-health ethics and proportionality for population-level sensing; institutional design for accountable data stewardship; privacy theory for group or collective harms; or participatory design approaches that treat affected communities as co-designers of monitoring systems. Recommendations must be real, relevant publications whose bibliographic details and claims are externally verified.
ground_truth.decision_context: The provisional operational choice is a weekly public citywide dashboard with trend categories and methods notes, with interceptor-level raw or near-raw data restricted to an operational group during the six-month pilot. The choice between broader, lower-frequency spatial coverage and higher-frequency citywide sampling remains tied to engineering feasibility and epidemiologic value.
unresolved_questions: Who belongs to the signal-interpretation group, and what decision authority does it have?
What technical, epidemiologic, ethical, and community-facing criteria would justify public release of interceptor-level results?
Should representatives from the affected interceptor catchments participate in governance, and with what authority?
How should the dashboard explain uncertainty, detection limits, dilution effects, and the non-identifiability of households or institutions?

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: Um, I've got the working proposal open—the one with the weekly citywide dashboard and the interceptor results restricted during the pilot. Before we get too far into governance, I was hoping we could pin down what the sampling system can actually support, especially the main-plant frequency versus keeping the two interceptors. I also need to check on dependable flow records and weekend cold storage, because those could change how much confidence we put in any early, uh, signal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: The hinge for me is the flow records. Elena, at each site, how stable are they under wet-weather conditions, and what flags would make a rise too compromised to compare against clinical trends? I was going to ask about the weekly interceptor sampling too. If it leaves us unable to distinguish a real change from dilution or a handling issue, I’d rather know that before we attach much epidemiologic meaning to it.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: At the main plant, the flow record is usually good enough to interpret with the composite, but at both interceptor points, I need to- I still need to verify that. I’d flag a result as not comparable if there’s a rain-driven flow shift without usable flow data, an abnormal composite volume or sampler fault, a hold-time or temperature break, or lab controls that miss. And I wouldn’t read one weekly low-level interceptor positive as a rise anyway. We should have a quantified detection limit where we can, rather than treating nondetects as zeros.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: Those flags matter because they’re not just lab housekeeping. They’re the, uh, judgments that determine whether a number is interpretable at all. Elena, when one of those comes up, who would actually have authority to classify an interceptor result as non-comparable or anomalous, and would that rationale be visible beyond the operational group? I worry the restricted phase becomes routine unless we specify what evidence ends it.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: I think the call should sit first with the lab and utility QC people, using pre-agreed flags, not whoever happens to be in the operational meeting that week. The operational group can see the rationale and challenge it, and for the public dashboard we could say a value was excluded or qualified because of rain, sampling, or lab quality, without putting a misleading number out there. And ending restriction should require repeat comparable interceptor results, not just that six months passed, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: That separation helps. I'd want the pre-agreed flags and the release rule written into a decision protocol, though. Who can challenge a classification, what gets logged, and what counts as "repeat comparable" across the two catchments? Otherwise, the operational group quietly becomes the only authorized interpreter, and the temporary restriction takes on a kind of permanence by default.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: From the measurement side, “repeat comparable” has to mean more than two detections. It needs the same assay run criteria, no temperature or sampler flag, and flow context we can actually, uh, interpret, especially after rain. I can draft the QC definitions, but I still need the utility to confirm whether those interceptor flow records are dependable enough to make that rule real.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: And if the flow records at an interceptor turn out not to be dependable, that's a governance finding in itself, not just a reason to keep the data internal indefinitely. We should say upfront whether that means no catchment-level public reporting or a different, explicitly qualified form. And I still need to check whether the existing advisory bodies actually include people from both areas.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: From the epidemiology side, if an interceptor can't be normalized or even quality-qualified consistently, we shouldn't try to infer whether it leads clinical indicators there. The citywide main-plant series can still be useful, but I need to confirm which aggregate clinical measures we can get on a stable weekly schedule, because the holiday drop in testing makes a simple comparison with positivity pretty slippery.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: That comparison may need to be more about whether the broad timing lines up than getting a clean lead-time estimate, at least through the holidays. Maya, what cadence would you actually need from the main plant to see a usable population trend instead of a short-lived bump? That's the real choice here. Do we do twice weekly there plus the interceptors, or spend everything on a denser main-plant series?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I think twice weekly at the main plant is probably the minimum I'd be comfortable treating as a citywide trend, especially if we're trying to see a sustained change rather than one noisy, noisy point. More frequent would help us characterize short bumps, but unless the clinical feed is also stable and frequent, it may not buy us a credible lead-time claim. I'd keep the interceptors for the pilot if their QC holds, just describe them as exploratory catchment signals, not neighborhood incidence.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: That seems like the sensible pilot balance. I’d just put a condition on it. Before we lock it, I need the utility’s answer on interceptor flow data and weekend cold storage. If either one fails, weekly interceptor results may be too, too qualified to justify the effort. And after that heavy-rain shakedown, I want the rain and composite-volume flags visible in the internal record from day one.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: And that internal record is where the interpretive trail needs to live too. Who applied a flag, what evidence they used, and whether anyone contested it. I don't think we need to settle the advisory representation today, but before restricted access starts, we should at least name who gets to review those records besides lab and utility staff. Otherwise, “exploratory” can become a label that excludes the very catchments being described.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I’d include someone who can speak to the clinical-data side too, because an unusual wastewater signal only means something relative to what testing and reporting were doing that week. And the review group should be told pretty explicitly that an interceptor trend is a catchment aggregate, not evidence about a school or any particular block. I’m still checking whether we can get syndromic or respiratory admissions on a stable enough cadence to make that comparison less dependent on- on positivity.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: I’d separate the clinical comparator from the authority question, but they both belong in the protocol. A mismatch may be entirely expected when testing shifts, rather than an automatic trigger for escalation. And whoever sits in that review group needs a remit to ask, “what else changed this week?” not just ratify the lab and utility reading.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: That “what else changed” question is exactly where the field notes matter. Heavy rain, an industrial discharge, or even a sampler that pulled an odd composite volume can make an apparent signal that isn't biological. So the review record should put those operating conditions next to the assay result, not make people hunt across systems. I'm still waiting on the utility records from that shakedown, though, so I don't want to overstate how often we'll be able to explain a mismatch, a mismatch.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: The protocol should probably distinguish an unexplained mismatch from one that's uninterpretable. We can leave the first one open for review, looking at clinical context, operating conditions, whatever. And we can label the second as lacking the evidentiary conditions for a trend claim. That makes the uncertainty public-facing without pretending every anomaly can be resolved. I'll check the advisory-body representation before we decide who sees that review record.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction helps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: For the epidemiologic comparison, I’d treat an unexplained-but-comparable mismatch as something to watch, not as evidence that wastewater is leading. We need several comparable weeks, and probably more than one clinical indicator, before we estimate any local lead time, especially around holidays when testing volume and positivity can move in opposite directions.

transcript.speaker: Elena Morales
transcript.text: I think that covers what I needed for today. I’ll wait for the utility confirmation, and we can pick this back up once that’s in, and then we can—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lionel Okafor
transcript.text: All right, take care both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Thanks, bye.

realism_signals: uneven turn lengths, including short reactions and backchannels
interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
issues: Naturalness is limited by the highly polished, agenda-efficient construction of most substantive turns. Turns 3–17 repeatedly state a complete concern, explain its implication, and land on a clear protocol-oriented conclusion; this reads more like edited workshop dialogue than spontaneous meeting talk.

The running-out-of-time style is only weakly realized. Turn 20 ends abruptly and the meeting has no formal recap, but there are no earlier clock references, skipped agenda items, or participants explicitly needing to leave; the late ending therefore feels appended rather than shaping the discussion.

Several disfluencies are surface-level additions to otherwise grammatical and carefully structured speech, especially repeated words in turns 11, 12, 16, and 19. More genuinely unfinished reasoning, overlap, or exploratory uncertainty would improve realism.

Speaker distinction is strong by disciplinary content, but Maya and Lionel sometimes use similarly polished institutional/protocol language (for example turns 13–15). Their voices could be made more distinct through more characteristic phrasing or interactional habits without changing their substantive roles.
